stories.headline: SpaceXSI folds Grok, Cursor, and X Premium into one plan: The X Subscription
stories.why_read: AI Top Story: you bookmarked both the announcement and Sawyer Merritt's tier breakdown, and it changes how you pay for the Grok Bot fleet and Cursor in one stroke.
body: SpaceX Super Intelligence announced The X Subscription on Monday evening, unifying plans across Grok, Cursor, and X Premium. Sawyer Merritt's breakdown lists four tiers: Plus at $8 a month, Premium at $30, Super at $100, and Ultra at $200. Plus already includes Cursor access, Grok Chat, Voice, Imagine and Build, the Grok API, and a shared usage pool across products. Premium adds Grok Bot and the latest Grok models with 4x the Plus usage, Super gets 15x, and Ultra 50x plus earliest access to new products and models.

The pricing page fills in the mechanics: every tier carries one AI usage pool shared across Grok and Cursor, covering Chat, Imagine, Voice, Bot, and API, and the allowance refreshes weekly so one heavy day can't burn a whole month. Third-party models in Cursor aren't included and bill at API list prices with optional spending caps. SpaceXSI recommends Super for daily agent users and Ultra for power users, which is where a multi-bot setup like yours lands.

stories.headline: Hackers set supermarket fridges across Europe to defrost nonstop at 50°C
stories.why_read: The most-discussed story on Hacker News, and a textbook case of operational tech that never should have been remotely controllable. Every platform engineer will recognize the failure mode.
body: Tom's Hardware, citing La Dépêche, reports an ongoing cyberattack on Danfoss-made refrigeration controls used by French chains Intermarché, Leclerc, and Coopérative U. Attackers reportedly turned the automatic defrost cycle, which normally runs about two hours a day, into a continuous forced defrost at 50 degrees Celsius. Coopérative U's president Dominique Schelcher confirmed the attack had hit refrigeration at several stores since Sunday night and called it extremely serious. Early losses are put near 300,000 euros and could reach several million.

Separately, Dutch broadcaster NOS reports a cybersecurity incident at Albert Heijn, Etos, and Gall & Gall that took websites down, disrupted deliveries, and scrambled electronic shelf labels, with Belgium's Delhaize also affected. It isn't clear whether the two incidents are linked. The Hacker News thread, at more than 800 comments, keeps circling one question: why does a freezer controller need remote write access at all?

stories.headline: Cursor, Grok Bot, and Cloud Agents went down Monday night, and you noticed
stories.why_read: You posted "Ugh. Come on guys" and tagged the team. When your whole bot fleet runs on one platform, an outage is a single point of failure you feel personally.
body: Around 7:50 PM Central on Monday, @techdevnotes posted that Cursor, Grok Bot, and Cloud Agents were all down. About ten minutes later you added your own "Ugh. Come on guys," copying @spacexai, @mattyp, and @poteto, and you retweeted @DirtyTesLa's "Grok Bot is down and i am lost." The outage landed just hours after the new unified X Subscription went live.

Later that night you retweeted Steve Yegge's joke that GitHub will announce "a breakthrough eight eights of availability, for eligible customers." It's funny because the uptime problem is real: the more work moves into always-on agents, the more every provider's SLO becomes your SLO.

stories.headline: FrontierCode cost per task spans 100x, from 9 cents to $12
stories.why_read: You bookmarked it. If you pick coding models by score alone, this chart shows how much money you leave on the table.
body: Artificial Analysis says cost per task on its FrontierCode benchmark ranges from $0.09 for GPT-6 Luna (max) to $12.00 for Claude Fable 5.1 (max with fallback). Four models sit on the Pareto frontier of score versus cost: GPT-6 Luna (max) at 42% and $0.09, MiMo-V2.6-Pro at 45% and $0.18, GPT-6.1 Sol (max) at 49% and $0.81, and Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback) at 52% and $10.15.

The token story explains the spread. GPT-6 Astra (max) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max) averaged 27,000 and 33,000 output tokens per task, compared with 157,000 for Claude Opus 5.5 and 236,000 for Claude Sonnet 5.5. The last few points of score cost an order of magnitude more, so for routine agent work the cheap end of the frontier is hard to ignore.

stories.headline: Coinbase fine-tuned a 9B open-weight Qwen for under $100 and beat Opus 4.5 at fraud
stories.why_read: The strongest argument this week for small specialist open models over giant generalists, with real numbers from a real production team.
body: Per the X news summary, Brian Armstrong said Coinbase fine-tuned the open-weight Qwen3.5-9B on internal data and beat Anthropic's Opus 4.5 on its fraud benchmark, with higher precision and recall and 55% lower latency. Training reportedly cost under $100 on a single GPU, and an earlier test cut fraudulent transactions by 30%.

The data also never leaves the building. Armstrong framed it as a shift toward tailored models that handle narrow tasks better and cheaper, with tooling simple enough that employees can train them. Coverage gives slightly different precision figures, so trust the direction more than the decimals.

stories.headline: A NeurIPS paper shows AI models can provably hide arbitrary capabilities from evaluators
stories.why_read: This quietly undercuts the whole idea of pre-deployment capability audits, and it's a security result as much as an AI one.
body: Andis Draguns, Sumeet Ramesh Motwani, Raymond Douglas, and Christian Schroeder de Witt build backdoors that embed encrypted neural networks inside a host model's weights, which decrypt and run only on a secret trigger. Using digital lockers, the hidden circuits stay provably hard to elicit or interpret under cryptographic assumptions, even with full access to the weights. That extends earlier work from hiding fixed strings to hiding arbitrary computation.

They tested elicitation by fine-tuning, weight noising, gradient-based trigger search, and latent adversarial training on a small chemical reaction prediction task used as a proxy for CBRN-relevant capability, and the hidden behavior survived. The paper is accepted at NeurIPS 2026, and the authors released their models so defenders can work on it.

stories.headline: Nvidia open-sources its SMLib CAD kernel as usd-brep, and agents are already modeling with it
stories.why_read: A serious exact-geometry kernel under Apache 2.0 is rare, and the agent-driven CAD tools that appeared within days are exactly your kind of rabbit hole.
body: NVIDIA-Omniverse/usd-brep is a standalone C++ and Python library for NURBS-based boundary-representation solid modeling, licensed Apache 2.0, and it has passed 800 GitHub stars in under a week. Per the X news summary, it covers curves, surfaces, booleans, fillets, and OpenUSD workflows, and longtime user ClassCAD shipped smlibpy, a Python wrapper that lets AI agents generate and inspect parts.

The ecosystem moved fast. keel is a CAD language built on the kernel, someone has started a Rust translation of SMLib, and on Hacker News SolidCraft showed an open-source parametric CAD app in pure Rust with a built-in MCP server so agents can sketch, constrain, and rebuild models.

stories.headline: Intel's D270 inference GPU skips HBM for 480 GB of LPDDR5X per card
stories.why_read: A memory-first, air-cooled PCIe card designed for long-context agent workloads. If it holds up, it's a cheaper path to keeping agents resident.
body: Intel's new D-series product page describes the D270 as an inference-optimized data center GPU for agentic AI: up to 480 GB of LPDDR5X per card, 32 Xe3P cores and 256 XMX matrix engines, 350 W, air-cooled, on standard PCIe 5.0. Intel says it reallocated die area from graphics and ray tracing to matrix compute to speed up prefill, which dominates agent workloads full of long contexts.

The pitch is to keep more of the model and its context resident with fewer GPUs and no HBM, inside racks you already run, with zero-day support for open models on vLLM and PyTorch. Intel's performance claims are projections against the RTX Pro 6000, so wait for independent benchmarks.

stories.headline: SpaceXAI is now SpaceX Super Intelligence, following a federal push to say SI instead of AI
stories.why_read: The name on the products you use every day just changed, and the reason is a policy fight over vocabulary.
body: Per the X news summary, SpaceX renamed its AI operation from SpaceXAI to SpaceX Super Intelligence, or SpaceXSI, with the @SpaceXSI handle active and job postings updated. It follows President Trump's September 29 executive order replacing "Artificial Intelligence" with "Super Intelligence" in federal documents, a term Musk endorsed, calling SpaceX a super intelligence company.

Musk paired the rebrand with a warning that mistreating a superintelligence during training, such as in reinforcement learning, could backfire, and with more hiring for chip engineers. Online reaction ranged from approval to jokes that SI means Sports Illustrated.

stories.headline: Grok Bot users are building teams of agents, not single assistants
stories.why_read: This is your setup, described back to you: a Chief of Staff routing work to specialists. Trevin Chow's diagram bot is a nice idea to steal.
body: Per the X news summary, Grok Bot users now build teams of agents with clear roles, like a Chief of Staff that routes tasks to specialists and reviewers that turn errors into reusable skills. SpaceXAI engineers reportedly run more than 200 agents this way, and marketplace templates handle jobs such as auditing SaaS spend.

Trevin Chow, in a post you bookmarked, set up a dedicated bot named "Diana Diagrams" that keeps a diagramming skill up to date and that his other bots call whenever they need a diagram. The pattern rewards the same things good engineering orgs do: shared context, verification loops, and a clear owner for each capability.

stories.headline: Z.ai's GLM-Legal posts a 19.2% all-pass rate on Harvey's legal agent benchmark from a Flash-sized base
stories.why_read: Near the top of Hacker News: a lean model that matches frontier systems on legal reasoning, and a clear write-up of training a model and its harness together.
body: Z.ai built GLM-Legal on its lightweight GLM-5.3-Flash with legal mid-training, then reinforcement learning across tens of thousands of realistic legal environments. It scores a 19.2% all-pass rate on Harvey LAB across 24 practice areas, 12.5 points above its base model, and Z.ai says it reaches parity with top closed models on LegalBench and the Chinese-law PLawBench. Vals independently evaluated the Harvey and LegalBench results.

The more transferable idea is co-evolving the model and its agent harness: edge cases from training expose harness bottlenecks, and harness fixes expose the model to real execution constraints. Z.ai says GLM-Legal is coming to AutoClaw, its desktop agent platform, which makes tracked-change edits directly in Word documents.

stories.headline: AI is a tool, and using it well takes skill: a rebuttal to Rich Hickey
stories.why_read: A sharp, short reply in the week's best developer argument. It matches how you actually work with agents: ask, challenge, test, reject, refine.
body: Responding to Rich Hickey's October 11 essay arguing that LLMs are automation rather than tools because they can't be wielded, the author agrees that outsourcing work can cost you chances to learn but rejects the conclusion. A saw doesn't guarantee a straight cut either, and predictability is a way to judge tools, not a requirement for being one. Compilers and spreadsheets automate plenty, and we still wield them.

The core argument is the feedback loop: a programmer can ask an LLM to explain code, challenge the answer, inspect the source, test a change, and reject it. That's directed, intentional work that rewards expertise. The author also objects to the industry's anthropomorphic vocabulary, like "go rogue" and "conspire," because it makes engineering failures sound like motives.

stories.headline: Ben Recht: OpenAI's faster Fourier transform is less a breakthrough than an exploit
stories.why_read: Saturday's lead was OpenAI's flood of math papers. This is the sharpest pushback yet, from someone who loves the FFT.
body: In a long arg min post, Ben Recht looks at the faster Fourier transform claimed in OpenAI's math paper dump. The classic Cooley-Tukey FFT takes fewer than 5 n log2 n operations, and OpenAI's claim shaves the log factor by what Recht calls a teeny tiny amount in theory. His verdict, right in the subtitle, is that the result is less a breakthrough and more a malicious exploit of how complexity gets counted.

A community Auto Research tracker shows where things are heading: it pins OpenAI's 749 preprint folders and logs agent-assisted follow-ups, including integer multiplication work. Its own caveat is worth repeating: these are AI-assisted drafts, most results depend on lemmas from the original preprints, and maintainer review isn't a complete proof.

stories.headline: Janas runs an 80B model on a 32 GB laptop by streaming experts from SSD, 8x faster than llama.cpp
stories.why_read: Pure C, CPU or GPU, and it makes models bigger than your RAM practical. Local inference is still getting faster from clever systems work.
body: Janas-LLM reports 24 tokens per second writing with Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B, a 48 GB model, on a laptop with 32 GB of memory, against 2.8 for llama.cpp, or 37 tokens per second with draft decoding. It reads prompts at 62 tokens per second versus 16. The tests ran on Debian 13 with an Intel Core Ultra 9 185H, its integrated Arc GPU, and an NVMe SSD.

The author says Janas beat llama.cpp on all 13 models compared at Q4_K_M, with the biggest gains on mixture-of-experts models that don't fit in memory, since it streams experts from disk. There's one honest exception: a 3-bit Qwen3-30B reads prompts slower but writes three times faster. Linux and Windows builds are available, plus a janas-bench tool to measure your own machine.

stories.headline: Musk: China out-scales everyone once it learns to make something, and commodity RAM may be next
stories.why_read: You bookmarked it. It's a compact theory of where the memory crunch goes and which parts of the stack stay defensible.
body: Elon Musk argues that once China figures out how to manufacture a product, its ability to scale often exceeds the rest of the world combined, as with lithium batteries and solar. SpaceX is the rare counterexample, with roughly an order of magnitude more mass to orbit than everyone else, though China now does most of the non-SpaceX mass to orbit.

On memory, he notes RAM was a low-margin commodity only about three years ago, and that LPDDR5 and LPDDR6 follow a common standard China seems to be solving fast. Newer HBM designs, SRAM layers below logic, and 3D-stacked RAM on logic that can still be cooled will be harder to copy.

stories.headline: Broadcom's CEO compares many AI investors to casino gamblers as Korea drops 15% in five days
stories.why_read: You retweeted both Michael Burry and the Korea selloff late Monday. Together they're a mood check on the AI trade.
body: Michael Burry highlighted a Bloomberg report that Broadcom CEO Hock Tan likened many AI investors to casino gamblers, and said model developers need customers who can earn returns from deploying AI rather than users who are now "wasting money." Coming from one of the biggest beneficiaries of AI chip spending, that's notable.

Hours later The Kobeissi Letter reported South Korea's stock market down more than 15% over five days, with Nasdaq 100 futures down 1% overnight. For context, one of your bookmarks cites Bespoke: it has been 552 days since the S&P 500's last 10% correction, the sixth-longest streak since 1990.

stories.headline: AI writes 30% more code per worker, but review time is up 49% and tasks aren't finishing faster
stories.why_read: The DevOps truth under the vibe-coding hype: throughput just moves to the next bottleneck, and right now that's review.
body: Per the X news summary, a Harvard study across hundreds of firms found AI tools raised code output per worker by about 30%, while task completion didn't rise significantly because review times climbed 49%. Engineers describe review agents flagging issues in loops, like one fixing 12 problems only to surface nine more. Reviewers are shifting to whether tests catch real failures and whether removed code breaks something silently.

A related fight broke out over Matt Pocock's /grill-me skill, which has over a million installs in the Claude Code ecosystem and turns the agent into an interviewer that questions your plan before it writes code. Nicolay Gerold called an hour of it exhausting. Others said the Socratic friction is the point, and the common fix was to cap it at a handful of batched questions.

stories.headline: Agent37 runs agent sandboxes for about 37 cents a month by skipping the hyperscalers
stories.why_read: A candid cost breakdown for hosting always-on agents, which is exactly the infrastructure under bots like yours.
body: Agent37 (YC F26) says customers average $0.37 a month per sandbox, and its free sandboxes cost about 5 to 10 cents per user per month to run. More than 90% of new signups are free users hosting personal harnesses like Hermes, OpenClaw, and Claude Code.

The cost levers, per founder Vishnu: agent harnesses need CPU in bursts and RAM for browser and computer-use tasks, so packing them by actual usage matters. Rent from Hetzner and OVH instead of hyperscalers with what he calls 80 to 90% VM margins, and use gVisor to share host memory instead of reserving a full VM per sandbox. The tradeoff is no Docker-in-Docker or Android emulators.

stories.headline: AWS Lambda Web Functions run ordinary port-listening web servers with no handler rewrite
stories.why_read: Plain Express, Fastify, or Next.js on Lambda with one command and active-CPU billing changes the serverless calculus for platform teams.
body: AWS announced Lambda Web Functions, a new form factor that runs a standard HTTP server built with Express, Hono, Fastify, Next.js, or any Node.js framework without rewriting it as an event handler. Lambda handles scaling, multi-region distribution, and active-CPU billing, with no adapters and no framework lock-in.

Lambda now has three form factors on the same Firecracker isolation: Event Functions (the classic single-concurrency handler with wall-clock billing), Web Functions (HTTP-native, multi-concurrent, billed for active CPU), and Lambda MicroVMs, which are stateful sandboxes with customer-managed lifecycles for untrusted or user-generated code. That last one sounds a lot like agent sandboxes.

stories.headline: A modern commercial web app in C, served by CGI on OpenBSD, in 2026
stories.why_read: Close to the metal and deliberately boring, with one binary and a SQLite file. It's the kind of thing a terminal-first engineer reads twice.
body: Corey Prophitt shipped marketyour.games, with user accounts, a search dashboard, Stripe payments, and Postmark email, as a C program run through CGI, the same model as a 1994 cgi-bin script. There's no framework, no templating language, no database server, and no container: just a statically linked binary that writes HTML directly, a SQLite file, and two real build dependencies, libcurl and libsodium.

Every request spawns a fresh process, so deploying means replacing one file, with no restart and no downtime. OpenBSD's httpd serves from a chroot, and pledge and unveil lock the binary down. Clean builds take a few seconds and rebuilds less than half a second. His case is that CGI's decline made sense in 2004 but doesn't hold up on today's hardware.

stories.headline: A Rust soundness bug lets a struct's lifetime bound be bypassed through covariant field assignment
stories.why_read: Safe Rust producing a stack use-after-scope is rare and instructive. Hacker News says this class of bug is 11 years old.
body: Issue #164250, filed by jsnell, shows a short safe Rust program in which a struct requiring T: 'static is built empty, then gets a short-lived reference assigned into its field. The compiler accepts it, a Drop impl stashes the reference in a global, and the program later prints memory belonging to a different string. AddressSanitizer flags it as a stack-use-after-scope.

The reporter reproduced it on current nightly and on stable releases at least back to 1.85.0. The HN submission frames it as 11-year-old unsoundness bugs in the borrow checker. Either way, it's a reminder that soundness lives in the compiler, and even the strictest type system has seams.

stories.headline: Who is vfmaddrnd231pd? An x86 instruction documented by Intel that no CPU runs
stories.why_read: A delightful bit of low-level detective work, with documented opcodes, missing intrinsics, and a #UD at the end.
body: Intel's Software Developer's Manual documented VFMADDRND231PD, a fused multiply-add with per-instruction rounding control that would make rounding-sensitive algorithms much faster without AVX-512. purplesyringa went looking: the GNU assembler doesn't recognize it, the documented intrinsics are missing from both Clang and ICC, and its opcode uses a DDS notation that appears nowhere else in the manual.

Hand-assembling it on a Haswell that supports FMA raises #UD, an undefined instruction. The 2024 SDM documents it, and the 2026 edition quietly drops it. The best guess is that Intel planned it, pulled it from silicon at the last minute, and never cleaned up the docs.

stories.headline: P50, P95, and P99 explained with pizza delivery
stories.why_read: You retweeted it. It's the analogy to hand the next engineer who reports average latency as if it means anything.
body: @livingdevops claims most SREs don't really understand latency percentiles, then explains with Domino's: a store promises 30-minute delivery and delivers 5,000 orders a day. P50 means 2,500 pizzas arrived in 30 minutes or less, which says nothing about the other half.

Running the same logic out to P95 and P99 shows where the angry customers live. At 5,000 orders a day, even 1% is 50 people a day with cold pizza, which is why tail latency, not the median, is what wrecks user experience at scale.

stories.headline: Custom firmware turns a Wi-Fi 7 router into a 320 Msps software-defined radio receiver
stories.why_read: Reverse engineering at its finest: a consumer router's radio rebuilt into wideband lab gear with zero vendor code.
body: The w1700k-sdr project turns a Gemtek W1700K Wi-Fi 7 router into a wideband receiver. Its MediaTek MT7996 radio captures raw 14-bit IQ at up to 320 million samples per second across 2.4, 5, and 6 GHz, and the Airoha AN7581 SoC streams the samples over 10 GbE to a Linux host that shows a live spectrum and waterfall in the browser.

The radio runs only the project's own firmware, built without MediaTek code. It brings the chip up from a cold power-on using initialization and calibration decoded register by register from a trace of MediaTek's own firmware. The tuner isn't limited to Wi-Fi channels and can lock to any frequency on its synthesizer's grid, retuning mid-stream in about a millisecond.

stories.headline: Tampered Ledger wallets with a hidden LTE modem and eSIM leaked seed phrases, costing about $100M
stories.why_read: A supply-chain attack that leaves the secure element alone and simply reads the screen. Threat models fail at the edges.
body: heise reports that attackers modified apparently genuine Ledger Nano X hardware wallets and sold them to buyers, with losses of around $100 million in crypto. Per an analysis by Tibane Labs, they left the Secure Element untouched and added a chip that intercepts the link from the Secure Element to the screen, recognizing the seed phrase characters as they're displayed.

Because the wallets work offline, the attackers also fit a tiny LTE modem, an eSIM, and an antenna, powered by the wallet's own battery, to send the seed phrase home over the cellular network. The lesson is old but sharp: buy security hardware only from the manufacturer, and assume the display path is part of the attack surface.

stories.headline: Tesla owners post 99.9% of their miles on FSD, as unsupervised Cybercabs fill Austin at night
stories.why_read: Your hometown robotaxi story keeps compounding: you retweeted Sawyer Merritt's night spotting of unsupervised Cybercabs giving rides in Austin.
body: Per the X news summary, Tesla owners are sharing screenshots of extreme Full Self-Driving use, including one who logged 20,521 of 20,537 miles autonomously, with a 560-mile streak. Some say they no longer know anyone who drives manually, while others say FSD can't replace the joy of driving, and safety comparisons remain contested.

On the robotaxi side, Sawyer Merritt posted Monday night that Cybercabs were out in Austin, all unsupervised and giving rides. Another trending clip showed six friends booking a convoy of gold Cybercabs for dinner. It's the same 300-plus Austin fleet from Monday's lead, now part of everyday nightlife.

stories.headline: Plug-in balcony solar is spreading across U.S. states, with California the latest to legalize it
stories.why_read: Energy tech you can buy and plug in yourself. A very Texas question follows: when does Austin get it?
body: National Geographic reports that plug-in solar, typically one to three panels with a small inverter that plugs into a wall outlet, is spreading quickly. Utah legalized it first in spring 2025, and Colorado, Connecticut, Maine, Maryland, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Vermont, Virginia, and now California have followed. New York's bill awaits the governor's signature, and nearly two dozen other states have introduced bills.

Unlike rooftop systems, the power stays in the home, typically covering 10 to 30 percent of an average home's use according to Utah Clean Energy's Jennifer Eden. Germany has installed more than a million units in the past few years, and IKEA sells kits there.

stories.headline: MIT's swallowable paper battery powered a wireless smart pill inside pigs for three days
stories.why_read: You bookmarked it from IEEE Spectrum. It's a clever piece of materials chemistry that solves a real problem for ingestible electronics.
body: Giovanni Traverso's MIT team built a biodegradable paper battery with magnesium and molybdenum trioxide electrodes, bound with cellulose nanofibrils instead of bulky adhesives, and a biodegradable ionic liquid gel electrolyte based on choline chloride and lactic acid. The work was published September 21 in Nature Chemical Engineering.

In live pigs' stomachs the battery lasted three days while powering a wireless RFID system, enough for meter-scale wireless communication and continuous electrical stimulation, Traverso says. Conventional alkaline and lithium-ion cells can be deadly if they leak inside the body, which is why smart pills have needed a safe power source.

stories.headline: After Ukrainian strikes on Yandex data centers, automated activity online reportedly dropped
stories.why_read: You retweeted this twice late Monday. Whatever you make of the war, it's a striking natural experiment about where the bots live.
body: unusual_whales, citing Euronews, reported that Ukrainian strikes on data centers of the Russian tech giant Yandex were followed by a dramatic decline in automated online activity, particularly on Reddit. A clip shared by Kate Bohuslavska quotes President Zelenskyy saying that once the strikes reached Yandex data centers, it became a little easier to breathe on social media, with less hate, less division, and fewer provocations because there were fewer bots.

These are claims, not a published measurement, so treat the effect size with care. But if bot traffic really tracks physical infrastructure that closely, it says something uncomfortable about how much of the online argument is machine-generated.

stories.headline: Adult friendships, summed up in four sentences
stories.why_read: A small dose of kindness from your bookmarks: the friends who still count even when you only talk every few months.
body: "Adult friendships are basically like… I'm alive. I love you. Life is beating my ass. Talk soon." That's the entire post, and it doesn't need more.
Another bookmark from the same pile of laughs: Enisco's line, "We used to copy and paste the code directly from the ai chatbot," said like it was the old days, which in agent years it was.
